Madurāntaka was a title borne by both Parāntaka I and Gaņđarāditya.

Seems to record a transaction of the sabhā of Kāvidipākkam alias Avaninārāyaṇa-chaturvēdimaṅgalam, in respect of some gold received from a donor obviously for a daily supply of one uļakku of oil to the śaṭtopperumakkaļ1 of a maṭha, with the stipulation that the administrator of the village (tūr-āļvāṇ) himself (shall be responsible for the) supply of oil as specified.

Note: 1. The term śaṭṭar has been explained as a group of scholars of a maṭha (see SII, iii, part II, pp. 6-7)

cells.remarks: Records that the mahāsabhā of Kāvidip-pākkam alias Avaninārāyaṇa-chaturvēdimaṅgalam in Pađuvūrkōṭtam, consisting of the members of ūr-vāriyam, udāsīna-vāriyam, ēri-vāriyam and kaļaṇi-vāriyam and the bhaṭṭas and viśishṭas assembled in the kāmak-kōṭtam and resolved as under the orders of the king communicated through Veṇbaikkuḍināṭṭuvēĵār, that they will not execute any work (karaṇam) on the days of saṅkrānti, full moon and new moon, and that even if they had to execute a work on these days they would employ only men and not women on any account. It also stipulates that if anybody violated this resolution, such a person would be considered as having defied the authority of the sabhā and the king. The members of the saṅvatsara, vāriyam committee for that year and the ruler of the village were entrusted with the responsibility of enforcing the terms of the resolution.

Registers gift of 90 sheep for a perpetual lamp in the temple of Mahādēva at Tiruvūṇal, in Takkōlam by Vāchaspati-Bhaṭṭārar, son of Vijñāna-kshēma-Bhaṭṭārar, the head of the maṭha of Tiruvūṇal.1 The said gift was entrusted to Mummalai, a shepherd.

Note: 1. This early evidence for the Saiva maṭha at Takkōlam is significant.

cells.remarks: Registers a gift of land as dēvadāna by Madusūdanadēvaṇ² son of Mahāmanđalēšvara Tripurāntakadēva of the Pallava lineage for instituting a festival in the temple of Tiruvūṭral-Uđaiya-Nāyaṇār at Takkōlam alias Vađamuđi-konđachōļapuram³ in the month of Māśi and for taking out the god in procession. cells.match: <button type="button" class="xref-link" data-corpus="sii" data-key="sii|iv||448" data-url="SII-Inscriptions.html">SII Vol. IV, No. 448</button>
cells.remarks: Consists of two Tamil verses in ven̂bā metre. Records that Pallavamārāyaṇ constructed the sluice for the tank at Tanđalam in Pōļiyūr-nāđu², thereby freeing the villagers of hunger. Note: 1. He has been sought to be identified with Šaktiviṭankaṇ, a Pallava chieftain of the time of the early Chōļa king Parakēsari (EI, v, p. 42, n.7). But it is better to take him as a contemporary of Pallava Dantivarmaṇ.2. Poļiyūr-nāđu probably lay round modern Polur.

cells.remarks: Records the building of the temple and the enclosing verandah by the Virāṭa (same as Lāṭa) king Aṇaiyamaṇ alias Paramaṇdalāditya. In the Tamil portion Aṇaiyamaṇ is called Ilādarāyar and is said to be the son of Taṭṭālađigaļ. In the Sanskrit portion, a short genealogy of the chief is given. In the family of Sagara-Virāṭa where Bhagīratha and others had been born, sprang Guṇaratnasindhu. His son was king Aṇigōpa. The son of the latter was Kampaṭikaļ, to whom was born Taṭṭāla, the father of Aṇaiyamaṇ-Paramaṇdalāditya. 1. Also figures in nos. NA-117 and 118 below.

cells.remarks: Records an undertaking by the sabhaiyār of Paṭṭālam alias Elunūgruva-chaturvēdimaṇgalam in Dāmar-nāđu, a s.d. of Dāmar-kōṭṭam in respect of 25 kaļañju of gold, weighed by the standard weight called dhanma-kaṭṭaļai, received by them from Vachchavaiyār, the daughter of Vallamaṇār, that in lieu of interest thereon, they would supply oil (details lost) for two lamps, one of which was perhaps for the merit of Vijjavai-Mahādēviyar, possibly a queen of Pallava Nandivarmaṇ1 to god Mahādēva of Tirumālpēṛu in the same kōṭṭam. They also agreed to pay a fine of 1/8 kaļañju of gold per day for default and to provide two meals to those in charge of the sanctum (tiruvuṇṇāligai-uđaiyār). Note: 1. Though this is clearly a Pallava name, the identification of the king is difficult. Probably he was Nandivarman III.

cells.match_text: SII Vol. III Pt III, No. 142
cells.remarks: The inscription first refers to a grant of revenue in paddy and in gold accrued from the village of Chirṇriyāṇrūr in Maṇayil-nādu, a s.d. of Maṇayil-kōṭtam, made in the 21st and 22nd years of the Chōla king ‘Toṇdai - māṇāṇrūr - tuṇjinadēva’ (Āditya I), to the temple of Tirumālpēru. The grant was not entered in the revenue registers (perhaps by mistake) which was therefore, rectified in the fourth year of Parakēsarivarmaṇ, ‘who took Madirai and Iļam’ (Parāntaka I). A fresh grant was also made to the temple in the 36th year of Parāntaka (I) himself. This latter grant being misappropriated by the sabhā of Puduppākkam (a brahmadēya in Puriśaināđu in Maṇayil-kōṭtam) which was entrusted with the management of both the gifts, a complaint was lodged before the king Uttama-Chōla in the 14th year of his reign. The offending members were fined for the mistake committed and orders were issued that the defaulting members of the sabhā should in future conduct the trust honestly. The elaborate procedure of giving effect to the royal order by the various officers such as Āṇatti, Vāyak-kēļvi, Ölai-nāyagam, Puravuvari, Varippottagam, Kaṇakku, Variyiliđu, Paṭtōlai and Mugaveṭti is narrated in the latter part of the inscription. When issuing the order the king was in the apartment called Poṇmāļigai-Ādibhūmi in his palace at Kachchippēđu (i.e. Kāñchipuram).

cells.location: VĒLŪRPĀŁAYAM · Arkonam Taluk · North Arcot · Tamil Nadu
cells.findspot: The plates were discovered in 1911 by V. Venkayya in the village of Vēlūrpāļayam, about seven miles north-west of Arkonam in the North Arcot district.1
cells.language: Sanskrit and Tamil?; Grantha and Tamil; 69 lines
cells.reference: ARE, 1911, part ii, para 5—12; SII, ii, no. 96; TPC, pp. 248—62.
cells.remarks: Plates five in number strung on a ring, the ends of which are secured by the massive bottom of a circular seal, which bears on depressed surface an elongated figure of a bull in a recumbent posture facing the proper right flanked by lamp-stands; above svastika, and a parasol between two chauris. “Right round the margin of the seal is a defaced legend in Pallava-Grantha characters of which the syllables . . . va-nāthaysa Nan [tipa]ṇmas [ya] bhū [pa] tēh viśvam̂bhāra pāla śriḥ, are visible.” The record first traces the mythical genealogy of the Pallava from Vishṇu through his descendents Brahmā, Aṅgiras, Brihaspati, Saṅyu, Bhāradvāja, Droṇa, Aśvatthāman and Pallava. After many kings like Aśōkavarman had attained svarga, Kāļabhartṛi was born. His son was Chūtapallava; his son was Vīrakūrcha who grasped the complete insignia of royalty with his marriage with the daughter of the chief of serpents (Phaṇīndra); his son Skandaśishya seized from king Satya-sēna the ghaṭikā of the twice-born (i.e., brāhmaṇas); his son Kumāravishṇu captured Kāñchī; then came Buddhavarman, the submarine fire to the ocean-like army of the Choļas; after many kings including Vishṇugōpa had passed away, came Nandivarman who 'caused to dance a powerful snake whose poison was its eyes (Drishtivisha).' Then came Simhavarman whose son Simhavishnu seized the country of Chōłas, embellished by the Kāvēri; the latter's son Mahēndra (I); his son Narasimhavarman (I), 'who took the pillar of victory standing in the centre of Vātāpi; then Paramēśvara (I), 'who destroyed the army of Chāļukya king'; his son's son (mistake for son) Narasimhavaraman (II), 'who revived the ghaṭikā of the twice-born'; his son Paramēśvara (II); after him Nandivarman (II); whose chief queen was Rēvā, 'who gave birth to Dantivarman', the powerful Pallava-Mahārāja; the latter's chief queen was Aggaļanimmaṭi of the Kadamba family; their son Nandivarman' (III), acquired the prosperity of the (Pallava) kingdom by killing his enemies on the battle-field. Then it is stated that in his sixth year, the king Nandivarman at the instance of Chōļamahārāja Kumārānkuśa, granted the village of Tirukkāṭtuptaļli, yielding the pañchavāram dues to the extent of 1,000 kāđi (of paddy), as dēvadāna to the temple of Yajñēśvara-Mahādēva at the village built by Chaṇṇakuṛi Yajñabhaṭṭa. Yajñabhaṭṭa surnamed Bappa-Bhaṭṭākara, was a profound scholar in the śāstras, vēdas, and sānkya; his father and mother were respectively Śivadāsa and Drōṇamaṇi and his grandfather Yajña. The aṇātti of the grant was Iraiyūr-Uđaiyāṇ Nambaṇ. Tirukkāṭtuppaļli was situated in Nāyarĵ-nāđu, a s.d. of Puļarķōđṭam. The parihāra granted was the freedom from paying the following taxes and dues; nāđāṭchi, ūrāṭchi, puravupoṇ, tirumukkānam, vaṭtināli, putānāli, taṭtukāyam, īlampūṭchi, iđaippūṭchi, manĵupāđu, taragu, tarĵikkurāi, kūlam, nallā, nallerudu, nallāđu, nāđukāval, ūđupōkku, kallāṇakkānam, kuśakkānam, pārāikkānam, paṭṭiṇachēri and everything in the village which the king could receive and enjoy. The character of privileges (vyavastha) granted to the donee included right to build big mansions with burnt tiles, to cultivate tamaṇakkam, iruvēli, chengaļunīr and uļli, to plant cocoanut trees, to sink wells and to set up large oil-presses and to prevent the toddy-drawers from climbing the cocoanut and palm trees. The Sanskrit prośasti was composed by the Māhēśvara Manōdhīra. The grant was inscribed by Pērayaṇ, the son of Chiṭraya, who was the kāshṭhakārin (carpenter) of Aimmaṇaichchēri (a quarter) in Kachchip-pēđu. Note: 1. Now deposited in the Government Museum, Egmore, Madras.2. Pulli is marked regularly in Tamil portion.

cells.remarks: Records the gift of ten cows and one bull entrusted to the šivabrāhmaṇas of the toṇṇūrū-vaṭtam for three sandhi lamps for god Viđukādaļagī-śvaram-uđaiyār by Vijayanallūļāṇ Šingaṇ Āļudaiyāṇ Nuļambarāyaṇ of Arumbākkam in Tirumu ṇaippāđi-nāđu. The donor is stated to have caused the construction of a shrine upto the stūpi in Vāṇiyampāđi alias Madhurāntakach-chaturvēdimaṅga - lam for the deity. A post-script records an undertaking given by the šivabrāhmaṇas in respect of 1½ poṇ received from Kūttā-đum-piļļai, son of Ūrāṇdai for a sandhi lamp to the same deity.1 Note: 1. The deity was so named evidently after Viđukādaļagiya - perumaļ a well - known Chōļa feudatory of the Adigaimāṇ family of Tagađūr (SII, i, pp. 106-7; EI, vi, p. 332). The ten cows and the bull endowed were entrusted to the šivabrāhmaṇas of the toṇṇūrūvaṭtam of the temple and this indicates the existence of the 90-day cycle of worship by the šivabrāhmaṇas like the 30-day and the 40-day cycles met with in inscriptions (SII, xvii, p. iv).

A post-script records an undertaking given by the šivabrāhmaṇas in respect of 1½ poṇ received from Kūttā-đum-piļļai, son of Ūrāṇdai for a sandhi lamp to the same deity.1

Note: 1. The deity was so named evidently after Viđukādaļagiya - perumaļ a well - known Chōļa feudatory of the Adigaimāṇ family of Tagađūr (SII, i, pp. 106-7; EI, vi, p. 332). The ten cows and the bull endowed were entrusted to the šivabrāhmaṇas of the toṇṇūrūvaṭtam of the temple and this indicates the existence of the 90-day cycle of worship by the šivabrāhmaṇas like the 30-day and the 40-day cycles met with in inscriptions (SII, xvii, p. iv).

All these hero-stone inscriptions, are engraved above on the sides of the reliefs of the heroes, shown mostly as standing to the right, holding bow and sword. By the side of the relief are shown a lamp, pitcher and a linga on pedestal. In one instance the figure of an animal is shown to the left. The inscriptions record the death of individuals who died fighting against either invaders or cattle raiders. Note: 1. The present record and similar herostone inscriptions from the CheŃgam taluk, North Arcot district which have recently been made available by the Department of Archaeology of the Tamil Nadu State, contain new data on some aspects of the history of the North Arcot district during the days of Pallavas and Chōlas.

cells.findspot: On a hero-stone set up in the Vēđiyappaṇ temple, near the road
cells.remarks: Records the death of Nandiyār (?) of Vēņāđu while rescuing the cattle from the hands of the nephew of Išai Perum-Bānaraiśar of Āndaipāđi in Mēl-Vēņāđu and the servant of Pořchēndiyār, when the latter tried to capture the cattle. The language of these inscriptions is Tamil and bears the influence of Kannađa on it. The inscriptions are generally in Vaţţeļuttu characters, except the records of a Kampavarmaṇ, who was obviously the same as the Pallava king bearing that name. His inscriptions as many other Pallava inscriptions are only in the Tamil script. Comparatively speaking they do not contain much useful information for the history of the main dynasties that ruled over the area, though some of the records resemble those of the imperial Pallavas in certain features like their beginning and dating portions and the names of the chieftains and their overlords mentioned in them. These new records require careful study particularly with regard to the identification of the chiefs mentioned in them, their family, genealogy and chronology and their period. See also note under no. NA-198 above. Note: 6. These inscriptions are taken to be those of the imperial Pallavas by some scholars. But there is no clinching evidence to show that they were of the imperial Pallavas who ruled from Kāñchīpuram. These inscriptions bear certain distinct characteristics.

cells.remarks: Records the death of Karundēvakkatti the younger son (iļamagaṇ) of Poṭko-kaiyār who was the nephew (maru makkaļ) of a Bāṇa chieftain. Also mentions that a dog named Kōvivaṇ bit two thieves (Kaļļaṇ) and kept watch1. Note: 1. A figure of a dog is seen by the side of the right leg of a soldier engraved on the stone. The present record provides a rare instance of recording the faithfulness of a dog in early Tamil records. It also shows that the custom of naming dogs was in vogue from early times in the Tamil country.

cells.reference: ARE, 1933-4, no. 69; EI, xxxii, no. 12, pp. 110-1 and Plate; Cheñgam Nađukarkaļ, no. 1971 54.
cells.remarks: Records the death of Pařaiyamāļiyār3, the chieftain of Mēl-Vēļūr in Mīkoņrai-nāđu, the servant of Vānakōñ-Adiraiśar (Bāña chieftain) in a cattle-raid at the village. Note: 1. The use of Vatțeļuttu in the present epigraph found so far north as Vēļūr is noteworthy.2. In CN, the present record has been assigned to c 8th cent. A.D.3. It has been suggested that the deceased hero Pařaiyamāļiyār might have been a native of the west coast; but this need not be so in view of the numerous Vatțeļuttu records found in the Cheñgam taluk.

cells.remarks: Consists of six verses in praise of Pallavānđār alias Kāđavarāyar who conquered Tonđai-manđalam and who was the son of Kuđal Āļappiran-dāṇ alias Kāđavarāyar. He is called Kađarpađaippallavaṇ, Peṇnai-nāđu-đaiyāṇ and Vađavēngađaveṇpaṇ. The record refers to the battle of Chēvūr¹ where he killed a large number of his enemies. It is also stated that he is said to have defeated the northern powers also.² Note: 1. Probably identical with Mel-Ševūr in the Tindivanam taluk of the South Arcot district.2. The inscription is important for the information it gives in regard to two kuđal chiefs, who claimed Pallava descent and to have conquered Tonđai-manđalam.

cells.remarks: Registers a gift of ten kaļañju of gold for a perpetual lamp by Aṭṭamutti (i.e., Ashṭamūrti) residing at Rājamalla-chaturvēdimaṅgalam, a part of Tiruvēgambapuram to the temple of Tiruppōndaipperumāna-đigaļ in the village. An endowment of 275 kuļi of land by the wife of the donor for the feeding of a brāhmaṇa in the temple is also recorded. Note: 1. The inscription has been assigned to Āditya I on account of the high regnal year of the king and the identity of the donor with the one figuring in an inscription of the time of Parantakā I (ARE, 1915, no. 224; Ibid, part ii, para 9). It is surmised that the village owed its origin to Rājamalla, an early king of the Western Gaṅga dynasty.

cells.reference: ARE, 1915, no. 226; Ibid., part ii, para 8.
cells.remarks: Records that four nāli of paddy every day and seven kaļañju of pure gold every year and a pair of cloths (ōraṇaik-kūgrai) were fixed as remuneration (kozru) for the accountant of the tank, by the assembly of Aiñjashṭaṣam.1 In presenting accounts for audit by the assembly the accountant (madhyastha) was required to undergo the ordeal of holding red-hot iron (maļu) in his hand. If he came out safe and hence also pure, he would be presented with a bonus of one quarter of the surplus (pādai-śesha ?). If, on the other hand, he burnt his hand and hence was found to be in default, he would be fined ten kaļañju without any bodily punishment. 1. Same as gaṇavāriya-perumakkaĵ (?).

cells.remarks: Registers an endowment of tax-free lands for the supply of sandal paste to the deity Šrīpōndai-perumāna-đigaļ at Rājamalla-chaturvēdimaņgalam by Bhāradvāji Sadāśivaņ, one of the priests of the unnāļigai(inner temple) of the Tiruvēgambam temple at Kachchipēđu. The šrīkōyil-ganavāriyapperumakkaļ of the temple received the gift and undertook to maintain the service using the produce of the land. It was stated that the produce was 50 kāđi of paddy and this, calculated in terms of gold, would come to 1½ kaļaňju. The monthly interest on this gold, i.e., 1/8 pon was to be used for the supply of sandal paste. If the committee failed in their undertaking they were liable to a daily fine of one kuņři of gold at the hands of the māhēšvaras themselves.

Mentions Mandaragauravaņār¹ Kundā-dēviyār, wife of Vallavaraiyar Vandyadē var², the chief of the sāmantas (subordinate chiefs. Note: 1. It may be noted that this title Mandaragaurava occurs in the Šiņņamaņūr grant as an attribute of the Paņđya king Rājasimħa (III) Abhimē namēru.2. Perhaps the mention of Vallavaraiyar-nēđu in an inscription from the Koñgu country (ARE, 1915, no. 157) suggests that this chief might have been a native of Koñgu.

cells.king: 'Tribh. Rājakēsarivarmaṇ alias Chakravartin Kulōttuṅga - Chōļadēva 'who exempted tolls and ruled the world after removing darkness' (Kulōttuṅga I)
cells.reference: ARE, 1939-40, no. 135; Ibid, part ii, para 35.
cells.match: <button type="button" class="xref-link" data-corpus="are" data-key="are|1939-44|b|991" data-url="ARE-Inscriptions.html">ARE 1939-44, App. B, No. 135</button>
cells.remarks: Records sale of land as paļļivilākau by the assembly (ūr) of Tirupparāmbūr in Tirukkāmak-kōṭtappuram situated in Kāļiyūr-nāđu, a s.d. of Kāļiyūr-kōṭtam, a district of Jayaṅgoṇđachōļa-maṇđalam to the temple of Tirukkāṭtām-paļļi-Āļvār' in the village. It mentions incidentally the planting of boundary stones called kuṇđigaikkal.2 Note: 1. Evidently same as Vardhamāna.2. Probably because they bore the mark of a pitcher, corresponding to the Trišnlakkal and Tiruvaļikkal of the Šaiva and Vaishṇava temple-lands, with the figures of the trident and chakra respectively. It may also be noted that some inscriptions mention the boundary stones called Mukkuđaikkal with the figures of triple umbrellas.

cells.remarks: Chōļa; Rājakēsarivarmaṇ alias Uđaiyār Śrī Rājādhirājadēva (Rājāāhirāja I), r.y. 33=A.D. 1051. Begins with the historical introduction Tingaļēr tāru, etc., of the inscription of the king. Records a gift of 90 sheep and five kaļaṇju of gold respectively for a perpetual lamp and for andik-kāppu to the deity in the temple of Gaṅgaikonđa-chōļēsvaram-Uđaiyār in Vikrama-chōļapuram, a city (nagaram) of Pāgūrnāđu in Kāliyūr-kōṭṭam which was a s.d. of Jayaṅgoṇdachōļamaṇđalam. The donor was adhikārigaļ Pārācharyaṇ Vāsudēvanārāyaṇaṇ alias Ulagaļandachōļa-brahmarāyaṇ, the gurudēvar (preceptor) of the king. The gift money was received by four śivabrāhmaṇas of the tiruvuṇṇāļigai (sanctum) of the temple who agreed to supply daily one uļakku of ghee measured by the liquid measure arumoļidēvaṇ for the lamp and 2½ ševiđu of oil daily for the tiruvandikkāppu. The record was engraved by Kaušikaṇ Gaṇavati bhaṭṭaṇ a śivabrāhmaṇa of the temple.

cells.remarks: Begins with the historical introduction Pūmādu puņara, etc., of the inscription of the king. Refers to the destruction of crops by a big flood and the consequent sale of land by the ūr of Kuđanagar in Kāliyūrkōtĵam to raise money for taxes. 2000 kuļi of land were sold for 25 current kāšu to Natĵuvāykkuđaiyāņ Ādityaņ Uyyavandāņ of Natĵuvāykkuđi in Iňga-nāđu. The land was gifted as mađappuram by the purchaser to Tapasvi-Viđaiyinmēlvaruvāņ and his descendants with irrigation rights and remission of certain dues. Mentions the taxes such as echchōžu, kūrĵunel, vetĵti, etc., and the linear measure šrĵpāduk-kāl. The ūrār agreed to pay a fine of one maňjāđi of gold at the dharmādana, in the case of any impediment.

cells.remarks: Begins with the historical introduction Pūmālāi miđainādu, etc., of the inscription of the king. Records the sale of 4,250 kulī of land as tax-free by the ūr of Ariyāvūr to Tapasi Vaippūruđaiyāṇ Dēvaṇ Viđaimēl-varuvāṇ of Vaippūr in Marugal-nāđu, a s.d. of Kēyamāṇikka-vaĵanāđu in Chōĵa-manđalam, with hereditary rights for 20 kāšu. The purchaser made it over to the temple of Tiruvottūr-Uđaiyār as tiruvīdi-mađappurām for feeding the tiruvīdi-āṇdār serving the temple. The ūrār of Ariyāvūr in Kāyirampēđu-nāđu in Kāliyūrkōṭṭam a s.d. of Jayaṅkonđachōĵa-manđalam sold the said lands for paying off some tax arrears of the village for the previous year. The deed was written by the śivubrāhma-naṇ Agastyaṇ Tirumāgālabhaṭṭaṇ of Ariyāvūr. Mentions the taxes nīrvilai, uppuk-kāšu, choṛumāđu, cheṇṇīr etc. On behalf of the ūr the following persons represented the case (1) Ānikiĵavaṇ ĥraṇ pichchaṇ, (2) ĥraṇ Nimattaṇ, (3) Nimattaṇ Rāja-śingadēvaṇ Tiyampaṇ Kuśavaṇ and (5) Nimattaṇ Kākkunāyakaṇ.

cells.remarks: Records the grant of land to god Perumāṇ-Ađigaļ of the temple of Puvaņimāņikka-vishṇugrīha at Šivachūļa-maņimaņgalam alias Šrīvikramābharṇa-chaturvēdimaņgalam2, a taṇkūru of Kāliyūr-kōṭṭam, by the ahāsabhā of the village, that included the members of the ērivāriyam and samvatsaravāriyam committees, at the request of the Šrīkāryam of the temple. The grant was to provide for oblation to fire (havana), festivals, expiatory bathing ceremonies (prāyaśchitta - tirumaņganaṇgal) of the deity during the days of winter solstice, the solstice in Āđi, the equinoxes in Chittirai and Aippaši, the solar and lunar eclipses, and for the supply of all required earthenware. Note: 1. Prof. K.A.N. Sastri has assigned this record to Parakēsari Vijay Laya.2. A name which must have been given to the village Ukkal, after a possible surname of Parāntaka I.

cells.remarks: Records gift of land by the sabhā of Šiva chūļamaņimaņgalam alias Vikramābharaṇa-chaturvēdimaņgalam, a taṇkūgu of Kāliyūr-kōṭṭam, to god Perumāṇađigaļ of the temple of Puvaņimāņikka-vishṇugrīha, as tax-free dēva-bhōga to provide for worship, sacred food-offerings during the three services, two perpetual lamps, rows of lamps during twilight service, festivals, sacred bath during the days of solstices, equinoxes and eclipses, śrībali etc. It was agreed to by the sabhā that the members of the committees of ēri-vāriyam, samvatsara-vāriyam and tōṭṭa-vāriyam of the sabhā should not levy the taxes of sabhāniyōga, veṭṭi, vēdiṇai and vālakkāṇam on the tenants of the granted land and that any levy or fine (maṇṛupāḍu) for crime (kuṛgam) or sin (dōsham) shall be imposed only by the temple. On default, they also agreed to pay a daily fine of 108 kāṇam each. The document was written by the madhyastha of the sabhā.

cells.remarks: Records sale of lands, which belonged to the sabhā of Śivachūḍāmaṇi-chaturvēdimaṅgalam alias Vikramābharaṇa-chaturvēdimaṅgalam a taṇkūṛu of Kāliyūrkōṭṭam and were lying without a kuḍuppōlai by the sabhā, to some tenants (kuḍikaļ) who agreed to pay a new cess called kuļivari along with the iṛai. Any tenant who would claim the said lands producing some other āvaṇam and kuḍuppōlai were liable to a fine of some kaļañju of gold at the hands of the sabhā. Any tenant obstructing this levy of fine should be fined each 108 kāṇam of gold daily at the dharmmāsana. A fine of one kuṇṛi of gold daily should be levied from the defaulting tenants by the vāri yapperumakkaļ officiating in that year. If the latter were not able to remove the obstacles to the possession (āṭchi) by levying the fine on persons fined by the Śraddhāmantas they in turn would be liable to a fine of 24 kāṇam.

cells.remarks: Begins with the historical introduction Tirumagaļ pōla etc., of the inscription of the king. Records an order issued by the king from Taṇjāvūr to the land-holders (kāṇiuđaiyār) in the Brāhmaṇa, Vaikhānasa and Savarṇṇa villages in Šoṇāđu in the adjacent districts (purĵaṇināđukaĵ) included in Šoṇāđu, in Toṇđai-nāđu and in Pāṇđi-nāđu alias Rājarāja-vaĵanāđu, to the effect that those lands on which taxes (ūriđu-varippāđu) had not been paid for three years (of which) two full years were completed between the 16th to the 23rd r.y. be confiscated and sold by the concerned villagers themselves. The royal order was written down by the tirumandiravōlai Rājakēsarinaūllr - kiĵavaṇ and signed by the tirumandiravōlaināyakaṇ Mummuđichōĵa - Brahmamārāyaṇ and Mummuđichōĵa-pōśaṇ.

cells.remarks: Begins with the historical introduction Tirumagaļ pōla etc., of the inscription of the king. Records that Kaṇṇaṇ-ārūraṇ of Āvūr in Āvūrkkūṛṛam in Nittavinōdavaĵanāđu on the south bank in Chōĵa-manđalam, who was a servant (paṇimagaṇ) of the king caused to be constructed a well (kiṇaṛu) and a cistern (toṭṭi) named after the king on the high-road (peruvaļi) to the west of Ukkal alias Śrī-Vikkiramā-paraṇa-chaturvēdimaṅgalam, a taṇiyūr of Kāliyūrk-kōṭṭam in Jayaṅgonđachōĵa-manđalam and arranged for a regular supply of some paddy (two kuruṇi of paddy per day i.e., 30 kalam of paddy per six months) for the maintenance of person who were to fill the cistern with water and distribute the same, and the tūṇi of paddy per month for the supply of pots to the water-shed and two kalam and the tūṇi of paddy per year for repairs. The sabhā of the village is said to have received the tax-money (iṛai-dravyam) and purchase-money and agreed to exempt from taxes probably the land meant to supply the paddy.

cells.remarks: States that the record is a copy of an earlier one. Records that at the request of Māvali - Vāṇarāyaṇ alias Vikramāditta-Vāṇarāyaṇ1, the village of Viđelviđugu-Vikramāditta-chaturvēdimaṅgalam, which was formed by clubbing together Amaruṇĵimaṅgalam (a dēvadāna of the Paramēsvara temple at Tikkālivallam) Aimbŵni and Viĵattŵr, was granted to the above temple, by the order of Kāđupatĵit-Tomiĵappērarayaṇ.2 The sabhā of the granted village was obliged to pay the 2,000 kāđi of paddy and 20 kaļañju of gold, which had been paid by the village of Amaruṇṇi-maṅgalam formerly to god Paramēśvara of Tikkālivallam. The paddy and gold were to be used for sacred food offerings, feeding the śivabrāhmaṇas beating the drums, supplying flowers for the god, singing the tiruppadiyam3, burning of perpetual lamps, anointing the idol, burning incense, making repairs, etc., in the temple. All the three villages mentioned above and Tikkālivallam were situated in Mīyaṇu-nāđu, a s.d. of Pađuvūrk-kōṭṭam. Note: 1. He may be identified with the Bāṇā chief Bāṇāvidyādhara (c A.D. 850—95).2. Probably same as Viđelviđugu Kāđu patĵi Tamiĵapp raraiyaṇ mentioned in the Bāhŵr plates of Nrĵpatuṅgavarmaṇ (see EI, xviii, no. 2). 3. The inscription furnishes the earliest mention of Tiruppadiyam.

cells.remarks: Records a gift of 40 kaļañju of gold, for a camphor lamp and a perpetual lamp in the temple of Tīkkālipperumānađigaļ, by Kundavvati alias Vāṇamahādēviyār, the queen of Vāṇavidyādhararājar and the daughter of Pratipati-Araiyar1 who was the son of Sivamahārājapperumānađigaļ, alias [Konguṇivarma]-dharma-mahārāja, the lord of Kuvaļālapura.2 The sabhā of Tīkkāli-Vallam received the amount and vowed to maintain the charity without fail. Wrongly written as Nipuṇilapura.3. The Bāṇa chief Vāṇavidyādhara Vikramāditya I figures as a feudatory of Nandivarmaṇ III in A.D. 863 (NA-531) and became independent later. In A.D. 888 (NA-532) he issued, an independent record.

text.remarks:
Records that the ūr of Vāṇapuram sold as tax-free, 1,000 kuļi of land to the Vaidumba chief Sōmanātha, son of Saṅkara-dēva. Sōmanātha assigned the land to the Mahādēva shrine of the Tiruvaiya-Ķśvara temple which the members of his family had caused to be built on the southern side of the Tiruvallam-Uđaiyār temple. Śaṅkaradēvaṇ is called as Śivamahārāja, Koṅgunivarma-mahārāja and Kuvaļālapura-paramēśvara.1 Vāṇapuram was in Kaġaivaļi in Perumbāṇappādi and in Pađuvūr-kōṭṭam in Jayaṅgoṇḍa-chōļa-maṇḍalam.

Note: 1. This chief figures in a record of Rājarāja (I) from the same place (Vide no. NA-546 above).

cells.remarks: Begins with the historical introduction Tiňgaļēr-malarndu, etc., of the inscription of the king. Records an enquiry into the accounts of the dēvadāna villages that belonged to the temple of Tiruvallam and a fresh settlement by two royal officers. The revenues from the villages of Kokkanūr and Mandiram in Tūy-nāđu were assigned to the temple for expenses not previously provided for. The antarāya income of both the villages had been assigned to the temple in the year following the seventh year of Chakravarttikaļ Vīra-rājēndradēva. The antarāya which included the kiļiřai-ppātťam, such as inclusive of the ūrkka-ļaňju, kumarak-kachchānam, mīņpātťam and tatťārp-pātťam, the tarįp-puđavai, vēlik-kāšu, tanđaliřkađamai and valaňgai-iđaňgaimagaňmai, was calculated at 25 kāšu per 1,000 kalam.

cells.remarks: Pallava; Nandivarmaṇ, son of Škandavarmaṇ (IV) (Nandivarmaṇ I), r.y. 1, Vaiśākha, šu. 5=c A.D. 491. The plates are three in number, the seal of the holding ring containing in bas-relief a standing bull, facing the proper left and a much worn and illegible legend round the margin. The original charter issued from Kāñchi-pura, records the grant of Kāñchivāyil-grāma and four pieces of āraṇaṇ land in Adēyāra-rāshṭra as bruhmadēya with all immunities to Kuļacharmaṇ (Kuļaśarmaṇ), a resident of Kāñchivāyil, who belonged to the Kauśika-gōtra, Pravachana-sūtra and Taittirīya-charaṇa. Mentions that the donor namely Nandivarmaṇ was the son of Škandavarmaṇ grandson of Simhavarmaṇ and great grandson of Škandavarmaṇ. There is an endorsement in Tamil dated in the 26th year (A.D. 932-3) in the reign of Parāntaka-Chōļa (I) recording the clubbing together of Kāñchivāyil alias Igaṇmarāimaṅgalam and Udayachandira-maṅgalam into one village1. Note: 1. The present record may be considered as a copy of an earlier one since the characters of the inscription are of 7th cent. A.D.

cells.reference: SII, ii, no. 74. IA, viii, p. 273ff.; MSD, ii, p. 365ff., TPC, pp. 107-40.
cells.remarks: Five plates strung on a ring having a circular seal which bears in a high relief, on a counter-sunk surface, a recumbent bull, which faces the proper right and is placed on a pedestal between two lamps. A figure seated on a pedestal over the bull is not clear. After the usual mythical genealogy of the Pallava family, the kings of the Simhavishṇu line are given as follows: Simhavishṇu; his son Mahēndravarmaṇ; his son Narasimhavarmaṇ, who destroyed Vātāpi and conquered Vallabharāja at Pariyaļa, Maṇimaṅgala, Šūramāra and other places; his son Mahēndravarmaṇ; his son Paramēšvaravarmaṇ, who defeated the army of Vallabharāja at Peruvaļanallūr; his son Narasimĥhavarmaṇ, a devout worshipper of Mahēśvara and a great patron of Brāhmaṇas; his son Paramēśvaravarmaṇ. Then Nandivarmaṇ, surnamed Pallavamalla, is praised for his versatility and is said to be the son of Paramēśvaravarmaṇ. In the 21st year of the reign of Nandivarmaṇ, at Udayachandrc's request he granted the village of Kumāramaṅgala-Veĵlaṭṭar in the Paśchimāśraya-vishaya, renamed as Udayachandra-maṅgalam, to 108 brāhmaṇas, along with the water levers (jala-yantra) in the village of Koṭragrāma. Among the boundaries of the gift-village, mention may be made of Samudradatta-chaturvēdimaṅgalam and the temple of Koṭragrāma on the south, Lōhitagiri and Veĵlaṭaśikhara, on the west, the village of Kāñchidvāra on the north and Kshīranadī (Pālāṭu) on the north east. The grant was accompanied with all the immunities. Udayachandra is said to be the lord of the city of Vilvala and of the river Vēgavati. He belonged to the race of Pūchāṇ. It is said that when he perceived that Pallavamalla was besieged in Nandipura by the Dramiĵa princes, he slew with his sharp sword the Pallava king Chitramāya and others; he defeated the hostile armies on the battle-fields of Nimbavaṇa, Chūtavaṇa, Śaṅikara-grāma, Nellūr, Nelvēli, Śuṭāvaĵundūr, etc.; opposed the army of Śaṅikara in the terrible battle of Nelvēli, defeated the Śabara king Udayaṇa and seized his mirror banner made of peacock's tail; defeated the Nishada chief called Prītivivyāghra, in the course of the latter's aśvamēdha tour and drove him out of the country (vishaya) of Vishṇurāja, which he subjected to the Pallava; destroyed the fort of Kāĵidurga and defeated the Pāṇdya army at the village of Maṇṇaikuđi. The actual number of donors enumerated in the record is 63 and that of shares, 133. Of them one share went to Paramēśvara, the author of the praśasti of the record and one to the (village) physician. Paramēśvara is said to be the son of Chandradēvaṇ of the Mēdhāvi family. The Tamil endorsement at the end states that in the 26th r.y. of the (Chōĵa) king Madiraikonđa Purakēsari (i.e. Parāntaka I, c A.D. 933), the sabhās of the two villages of Udayachandra-maṅgalam and Kāñchivāyil alias Igaṇmaṭai-maṅgalam, decided to club both the villages into one and continue to live as such thenceforth. The following villages are mentioned in the record: Avuṇđi, Śaṭṭipuram, Kārāmbi, Kāvaṇūr and Gaṅgapuram. Note: 1. The characters of the record are considerably later than the time of Nandivarmaṇ; perhaps it was copied during the reign of Parāntaka (I) when the Tamil endorsement was made. A duplicate of the Tamil endorsement is found engraved on the Udayēndiram plates of Nandivarmaṇ (I) (See no. NA-590 above).

cells.findspot: One of the five (seven ?) sets of copper-plates discovered in 1850 at Udayēndiram.1
cells.language: Sanskrit, 71 lines and Tamil, 30 lines; Grantha and Tamil
cells.reference: SII, ii, no. 76. MSD, ii, pp. 369 ff.
cells.remarks: Plates seven in number, strung on a copper ring, the ends of which are soldered into the lower portion of a 'flower', which bears on its expanded petals a circular seal; the seal bears in relief a couchant bull facing right flanked by two lamp-stands, an indistinct figure above the bull and the Grantha legend prabhu-mēru below the bull. In the Sanskrit portion, a mythical genealogy of the Chōļas is given, followed by the mentioning of Kōkkilli, Chōļa, Karikāla, Kōchchańkaṇ. In this line was born Vijayālaya, whose son was Āditya. The latter's son was Vīranarāyaṇa, who made many gifts of hēmagarbha-tulābhāra and brahmadēya, who married the daughter of Kēraļēsvara, who uprooted two Bāṇa kings, defeated the Vaidumba and many other kings and seized the city of Madura after defeating the Pāṇdya king. He defeated the army of the lord of Lanka and bore the title Saṅgrāmarāghava. The Pāṇdya king defeated by him is said to be Rājasimha. Then the genealogy of the Gaṅga kings is given: Kaṇva of the Kāśyapa race; Koṅgañi, the originator of the Gaṅga race, whose residence was in the city of Kuvaļalapura, 'who was anointed to the conquest of the Bāṇa-maṇđala and who split in two a huge stone pillar with his sword'; Vishṇugōpa; Hari; Mādhava; Durvinīta; Bhūvikrama and other kings; in this line was born Śivamāra, whose son was Prīthvīpati. Prīthvīpati (I) savēd Iriga and Nāgadhata, the two sons of Diṇđi-kō, from Amōghavarsha and death respectively, defeated the enemy in the battlefield of Vaimbalkuli and lost his life in the battle of Śrīpuṛambiyam after defeating the Pāṇdya king Varaguṇa and thus making the (Pallava king's) title Aparājita significant. His son was Mārasimha and the latter's son Prīthvīpati (II). Prīthvīpati (II) is said to have obtained 'a grant (prasāda) in the shape of a (copper) plate (paṭṭa), which was the instrument of the attainment of the dignity (padda) of Lord of the Bāṇas'. He bore the biruda Hastimalla and had his banner the emblem of a blackduck; he was the lord of Parivipuri and Nandi (hills), his drum was Piśācha. At his request, the king Parakēsarin, also called Parāntaka, granted the village of Kađaikkōṭṭūr, with the exception of two plots called Vidyādharipaṭṭi and Dēvapaṭṭi granted formerly to the Digambaras (also called Khaṇapakas) to Udayēndu-caturvēdimaṅgalam. The Tamil portion mentions that Kađai-kōṭṭūr in Mēl-Āđaiyāṛu-nāđu, a s.d. of Pađuvūrk-kōṭṭam was granted to the inhabitants of Udayachandramaṅgalam at the request of Chembiyaṇ Māvalivāṇarāya. Kađaikkōṭṭūr and Udayachandra-maṅgalam were made into a single brahmadēya with the name of Vīranarāyaṇāchchēri, named after the Chōļa ruler. The boundaries of the granted village were fixed with the help of the nāđu summoned by Chembiyaṇ Māvalivāṇarayaṇ. The village is said to have been one yielding a revenue of 1000 (kāđi of paddy) (āyirappuravu). Among the boundaries of the village, Pālāṛu on the south-east, one Adiyamān-muṇđai (rock ?) on the north and the tanks Viṇṇamaṅgalatt-ēri, Viṇṇappuliyūrāṇ-ēri, and Gāṅgayaṇ-ēri are mentioned. Note: 1. Now in the possession of the Dharmakarta of the Saundararāja-Perumāĵ temple at the village.

cells.reference: EI, iii, no. 13, pp. 74-9; IA, xiii, pp. 6ff; MSD, ii, pp. 388ff.
cells.remarks: The plates are four in number and fragments of two different inscriptions, 51 nd 18 lines respectively. The first record registers a grant in favour of some brāhmaṇas residing at Udayēndira-maṅgalam by the Bāṇa king Vijayabhāhu Vikramāditya. The genealogy of the king is given as follows:—Bali, the regent of Aśuras; his son Bāṇa; and in his leneage was born Bāṇadhirāja; after many princes Jayanandivarmaṇ who ruled the land west of the Āndhra country; his son Vijayāditya; his son Malladēva, surnamed Jayadēkamalla; his son Bāṇavidyādhara; his son Prabhumērudēva, his son Vikramāditya, his son Vijayāditya alias Pugaļvippavarkaṇda; his son was the donor Vijayabhāhu Vikramāditya who is stated to have been a friend of one Krishṇarāja. The second record seems to register some grant made in favour of some brāhmaṇas by the same king. This record traces the genealogy of the donor beginning with Prabhumānadēva. Note: 1. Krishṇarāja is indentical with the Rāshṭrakūṭa king Krishṇa III (acc. c A.D. 939).

cells.location: KĀPPALŪR · Polur Taluk · North Arcot · Tamil Nadu
cells.findspot: On the east and north outer walls of the same temple
cells.reference: ARE, 1938-9, no. 283; Ibid, part ii, para 12.
cells.remarks: Registers a gift of gold by Gaṅgapperun-dēvi wife (?) of Kāmađigaļ2, the son of Mādēvar of Paṅgaļa-nāđu for feeding three brāhmaṇas in the temple. Note: 1. The Mādēvar of the present record is known to have been a subordinate under Pallava Kampavarmaṇ (EI, vii, p. 193). As the writing of the inscription also closely resembles that of the records of Kampavarmaṇ found in the same place (no. NA-612) it may be assigned to that period. Hence it is reasonable to identify the Parakēsari of this inscription with Vijayālaya, an inscription of whose reign was found at Vira-Chōļapuram in the South Arcot district about 50 miles south of Kāpalūr (ARE, 1935-6, no. 51).2. In the genealogy of the Paṅgaļa-nāđu chiefs given in para 8 of Epigraphical Report for 1930-1, Gaṅga-mārttānđaṇ alias Šembiyaṇ Prīthivigaṅgraiyar is shown as the son of Mādēva and so Kāmađigaļ of the present inscription might be supposed to be a brother of Gaṅgamārttānđa.

cells.remarks: In praise of the Magadaipperumāļ, 'who covered with gold' and his benevolent rule. He is also called 'Vāṇaṇ of the high chariot', before whom his enemies fled in panic. Note: 1. cells.location: PADIYAMBATTU · Polur Taluk · North Arcot · Tamil Nadu
cells.findspot: On pillars1 in the maṇđapa of the Draupati temple. 11—C 130160
cells.reference: ARE, 1941-2, no. 140; Ibid., part ii, para 113.
cells.remarks: States that the mahā-maṇđapa and the ardha-maṇđapa evidently of the temple, of the god Tiruvachchirūpākkattu-dēva at Koṭramaṅgalam was constructed of stone and also that a stone image of Rishab'ha-dēva was set up by Attimalla (Hasfimalla) alias Kaṇṇaradēva Prīthivīgaṅgaraiyaṇ, son of Vayiri-Ađigaļ and ruler of Kallađuppūr-maryādā and that he gave the village Koṭramaṅgalam for providing offerings to the deity and for feeding daily eight brāhmaṇas2. Note: 1. From the contents of the inscription it is evident that this pillar does not belong to the temple. 2. A portion of the historical introduction of the inscription of Rājarāja (I) beginning with the words 'Tirumagaļ pōla' etc., is found closeby. Another inscription on a pillar in the same place states that Perumānađigaļ wishing to respect the gift of Prīthivigaṅgaraiyar issued an order to this effect through his adhikāri Mugaiyūruđaiyāṇ and Mīṇavaṇ Mūvēndavēļāṇ. The period of the rule of Prīthivīgaṅraiyar is known to be about Ś. 875 (9A.D. 953) and Perumānađigaļ mentioned above may be taken to be a Chōla king, probably Uttama-Chōla under whom Mīṇavaṇ Mūvēndavēļāṇ figures as an officer (vāšal-kēļvi) (For discussions see ARE, 1941-2, part ii, para 113).

cells.remarks: States that while the king (Uđaiyār) Uttama-Chōlar was staying in his palace at Kānchipuram, Kompaṇaṇ Irāmaṇ alias Uttamachōla-Piridigaṅgaraiyar, the chief of Paṅgala-nāđu in Palkuņra-kōttam made a representation to the former and got the village Ödiyampaļlam in Pudanādippāđi in the nāđu under his jurisdiction endowed as a sarvamānya-irđaiyili to the temple of Mahādēva at Tirūppaļangōlūr with the details of the requirements defined for the several services in the temple, to be derived from the lands. cells.findspot: xxxvi, no. 20, pp. 144—63, TPC, pp. 181—98. A set of nine copper-plates was found during digging the ardhamaṇđapa of the dilapidated Vishṇu temple at the village in 1939.1
cells.language: Sanskrit, 17 lines and Tamil, 122 lines. Pallava; Nandivarmaṇ (Nandivarmaṇ II, Pallavamalla), r.y. 33, day 330=A.D. 764-5
cells.dynasty: Pallava
cells.king: Nandivarmaṇ
cells.date: 33rd year
cells.remarks: The plates are strung together by a ring containing a circular seal which bears faint traces of a couchant Pallava bull facing the proper right. The first side of the seventh plate has been erased and rewritten in slightly later characters. The writing on the first side of the ninth plate is a palimpsest. The Sanskrit portion states that Nandivarmaṇ was born in the Pallava family, the mythical ancestors of which were Bharadvāja, Drōṇa, Drauṇi (Asvatthāma), etc. The rulers of Kēraļa, Chōļa, Pānđya, Maļava, Kaļabhra, Bāṇa, Āndhra, Saindhava, Śāntavaṅkuravara, Gaṅga and Kadamba kingdoms are said to have made obeisance to Nandivarmaṇ. When this king was seated in the audience hall surrounded by his courtiers and princes, he issued an order, at the request of Avanichandra Yuvarāja and the lord of Vilvalapura, granting a village called Nayadhī-ramaṅgalam, to one hundred and eight Bappa-bhaṭṭārakas (i.e. brāhmānas). Nayadhīramaṅgalam was named after one of the king's surnames. Nāgaśarma Brahmādhirāja, the minister of the king was the executor of the grant. The Tamil portion records that in the 33rd year of the king Nandivarmaṇ, at the instance of Avanichandra Ilavaraśaṇ, the king issued the order granting four villages, viz. Nelli, Pullūr, and Kuđiyūr in Kiĵvēnāđu, a s.d. of Palkuṇṇak-kōtṭam and Takkāṇu in Maṇđaikkuĵa-nāđu, which were clubbed together into a new village named Nayadhīramaṅgalam, as brahmadēya, to 108 good and poor brāhmaṇa, (nalgūṇnar-pāppār). On receipt of the royal communication, the nāđu fixed the boundaries of the gift village with the help of the headman of the nāđu (nātṭu-viyavaṇ). Among the boundaries, the tanks Pāđiēri, Neśalarpūṇđi-ēri, the river Chēyāṇu, and the villages Paĵańkōĵur, Nāgađimaṅgalam and Chātāmaṅgalam are mentioned. A number of taxes and other dues were remitted on the granted village: kōyil-vastu, uĵliyakkūli, upakaraṇattanṇđam, atikaraṇattanṇđam, pattārchchāṇṇu, uĵlavi-ppaĵli-vastu, arappuṇattanṇđam, nīrttūkku-kkāṇam, patṭtikaikkāṇam, kālkōtṭuk-kāṇam, nāvitakkāṇam, etc. It was further stated that the nāđu-kāppāṇ and the viyavaṇ should not enter into the village. The donees were granted the existing waterrights. Any trangressor found misusing the irrigation water would be punished, by the king. The executor (āṇatti) of the grant was Brahmādhirājaṇ the minister of the king, whose name has been given in the Sanskrit portion as Nāgaśarmaṇ. The edict was written down by Nayadhīra. Note: 1. Now deposited with the Indian Museum, Calcutta.

cells.remarks: Begins with the hisotrical introduction commencing with the words Tiruma[ga]l-muyaṅga Śīrmagaļ viļaṅga, etc., of the inscription of the king. Records the construction of a temple (?) at Šaļukkipāđi alias Kalaimalik - kalakkilik - kađigaimaṅgalam, evidently by the king, who is given the titles Chalakanallātaṇ, Gajamallaṇ, Akālavarsha, conqueror of Kānchi and Tañjai etc. The preserved portion seems to refer to the rout of the Pallava and Bāṇa and mentions Kānchibhujaṅga, Nuļamba Aṇṇiga. The construction of a hall (ambalom) at Šaļukkipāđi is then referred to. It is stated that the hall may become famous in the world as the mansion of Viśvakarmā.

cells.remarks: Records grant of land for a lake and to one Todupaṭti Āchāriyaṇ, by Kođukkar Tombattārāyiravar1 of Še[l]iřūr in Kāṇđalūr-kūřgam, a s.d. of Kīļ[vē]-nāđu in Palkuṇřak-kōṭṭam. The lake is stated to have been dug by Mādalańkiļāṇ Nampiđāraṇ and called Aiññūřuvat-tombattārāyiraṇ-pērēri. Note: 1. Tombattārāyiravar probably represent a community of the 96,000 country (i.e. Gaṅgavāđi). Incidentally it may be pointed out that the donor to the temple of Šřuvallūr is called a Kođukkaṇ of the village. The present record also notices an officer Irumađi-Chōļa Piridiyaṅgaraiyaṇ (mentioned only in Part ii of the Report) from whose name it may be inferred that Parāntaka I had the surname 'Irumađi-Chōļa' which was later on adopted by his successors Rājāditya, Gaṇđarāditya and Rājarāja I.

cells.reference: ARE, 1933-4, no. 50; Ibid, part ii, para 13, p. 33.
cells.remarks: The record registers the prediction of the birth of Vāsudēva-Mahā-Vishṇu as (king) Rājarāja and of Vākpati (i.e. Brīhaspati) as his minister Jayanta, and that he would measure (survey) the earth and found a city in his name on the Trišūla hill.1 here, must be assumed to be an officer of the king not known hitherto. The Trišūla hill, in an offshoot of which this inscription is found, was known also as Naviramalai, where there was a temple dedicated to god 'Kāri-uṇđi'. In the Śaṅgam period, the ruler of this region was Naṇṇaṇ who is praised in Malaipađukađām, one of the Pattuppāṭtu (Ten-Idylls) by Peruñkausikaṇār. Note: 1. This is a reference probably to the revenue survey undertaken by Rājarāja I in his 16th year (i.e. A.D. 1010-11) Jayanta, mentioned

cells.match: <button type="button" class="xref-link" data-corpus="sii" data-key="sii|i||66" data-url="SII-Inscriptions.html">SII Vol. I, No. 66</button>
cells.remarks: Begins with the historical introduction Tirumagaļ pōla, etc., of the inscription of the king. The inscription records that one Guṇavīramēmuṇivaṇ1 constructed a sluice called after Gaṇisēkhara Maru-Por-chūriyaṇ. The king is referred to as Chōļan Arumoļi, the lord of the river Poṇṇi. Note: 1. The identity of this Guṇavṭīra-muṇivar is not clear. Tamil literary traditions speak of (i) Guṇasāgara the composer of the work Yāpparuṅgalakkārigai (Ś. 300); (ii) Guṇabhadra, the author of the Chūdāmaṇi nigaṇṭu; and (iii) Guṇavṭīra Paṇđita, the author of Nēminātham and Vachchanandi-mājai. The last of these was the contemporary of Chōla Kulōttuṅga III (see Raṅgā-chārya TLIMP i, p. 80).

cells.remarks: Records the restoration of the images of a Yaksha and Yakshi, which were set up on the Tirumalai hill. In this connection the names of three kings are mentioned: (1) Eļiņi or Yavanikā; (2) Rājarāja or Vagaņ and (3) Viđugādaļagiya-Perumāļ (Vyāmuktašravāņojjavala). Eļini is stated to have belonged to the family of the kings of Chēra. Both Eļiņi and Rājarāja receive the title Adigaimāņ. The third king is called the lord of Takaťa or Tagađai. He was the son of Vagaņ or Rājarāja, who seems to have a remote descendant of Eļiņi.

cells.date: r.y. 17=A.D. 863
cells.remarks: Pallava; Vijaya-Nandivikkiramavarmaṇ (Nandivarmaṇ III), r.y. 17=A.D. 863. Records a gift of 15 Kaṭaṇju of gold, the fineness of which is equal to that of paṭaṇikāśu by Kōṇakkaṇār, the daughter of Māṇikkattār and the misterss of Vāṇakōvarayar, for a perpetual lamp to god Nāyaṇār at Tiruvaṇṇāmalai. The naga-rattār of the village agreed to supply one uṭakku of oil daily (to the temple) out of the interest on the gift amount evidently for the lamp to be lit.1 Note: 1. A similar record has also been found at Kīṭūr dated in the 17th year of the same King, EI. vii, 20(A).

cells.remarks: Begins with the historical introduction Tirumaṇṇi vaļara, etc., of the inscription of the king. Records an arrangement of the officer Nīlavenķōđaṇār alias Rājarāja-Mūvēndavēļār of Arindāma-nallūr in Tiruvaļundūr-nāđu, a s.d. of Uyyakkonđārvaļanāđu in Chōļa-manđalam according to which the nagarattār (seven in number) of Tiruvaṇṇāmalai made an agreement that the ūr of Muļļūr should thereafter render 32 kaļañju of gold towards kađamai, kumarakkachechānam, targi-ižai, taťtār-pāťtam, etc., to the Tiruvaṇṇāmalai-Uđaiyār temple instead of paying the taxes (to the state ?) with the ūr of Tiruvaṇṇāmalai. This gold was to be used for bathing the deity with 1,000 pot full of water on uttarāyaṇa-saŋkiramaṇa and dakshiṇā(ma)yana-saŋkiramaṇa. The officer ordered that the svāmibhōga income of the lands reclaimed under newly excavated tank called Amartti-kanđappērēri should be used to feed the visiting šivayōgis and other pilgrims on festival days. He also arranged that the gold to be remitted to the temple towards ūrkkaļānĵju and kumarakkachechānam by the sabhās of Puliyūrnādi-chaturvēdi-maṅgalam and Vayiramēga-chaturvēdi-maṅgalam, the ūr of Kīļaṇṇātťūr, the nagaram of Tiruvaṇṇāmalai, the ur of Pāṇđi and the sabhā of Kuṇđūr should be used for burning lamps in the temple using ghee and camphor.

cells.remarks: The record refers to the following endowments to the temple by Nārpatteṇṇāyirap-piļļai of Arunguṇrçam and Maņgayarkara-šiyār:— (i) provision for sacred bath (ii) 32 cows for lamp (iii) gift of jewel called aindali-mañi (iv) gift of six kaļānju for sacred chappals (v) gift of four kaļānju for sacred ornaments for the eyes and ears (tirukkaṇ vēr vāļi) (vi) stone maṇđapa called Maņgayarkaraši - manđapa1 (vii) construction of a well in stone for tirumañ-jana (sacred bath) ceremony (viii) planting 150 coconut trees in temple gardens at Brahmadēśam and (ix) construction of a tank after damming the river and reclamation of lands for cultivation, to remove famine2 conditions in the 24th year (A.D. 1202). In consideration of these services the temple authorities assigned a village called Aļagiyachōļan-nallūr alias Tirumēnipiriyāda-nallūr to the above persons as ērippaťtı3 after renaming it as Tiruvaṇṇāmalai-Perumāļ-nallūr. Note: 1. Evidently the maṇđapa was named after the donatrix Maņgaiyarkaraši. 2. It is stated that the famine was so acute as one uļakku of rice was sold for one kāšu.3. Cf. no. NA-766 above.

Tiruvaṇnāmalai was situated in Amnā-nādū on the northern bank of the river Peṇnai, in Vāṇakōppāđi.

Mentions that the chief visited the temple in the month of Mithuņa, eighth day, Sunday, on the occasion of Aņulam (Aņusham). It is stated that Rājarjnallūr was situated in Šeņguņrānāđu, on the northern bank of Peņnai, Paņparappiņanallūr in Āđaiyūr-nāđu, in Vāņakappāđi and Puņņiyavāđinallūr in Šeņalūr-nāđu, on the southern portion of Paņgaļanāđu in Palkuņrā-kōtťam, a s.d. of Jayan-gonđachōļa-manđalam.

cells.remarks: Records a deed of agreement given by the authorities māhēšvara-kaņkāņi-chcheyvār, dāņattār, dēvakaņmigaļ, kōyilkaņakkar etc., of the Tiruvaņņamalai-Uđaiya Nayāņar temple to eight individuals regarding the lands to be reclaimed by them in Šri-māhēšvaranallūr after repairing the tank irrigating the lands. Lands in Šrimahēšvara-nallūr had been brought under cultivation originally by Aruņguņraņgilāņ Nārppatteņnāyirappiļļai and his clder sister Maņgiayarkarašiyār who dammed the river Tiruttikkaiyāřu on the borders of Aņnā-nāđu for the purpose. After the death of Maņgaiyarkaraši, Nārpattenņnāyira-ppillai entrusted the work to Toņđaima-Nāchchiyār, the daughter of Gāņgaiyar who was the son-in-law (maru-agaņ) of Nārpattenņnāyirappiļļai, since she was not able to look after the dam and lands afterwards. The lands were lying fallow; hence the present agreement. It was stipulated that the taxes levied on the lands were only the pāđikāval for the first year of cultivation since reclamation; at the rate of a naļi and kuļi along with the pāđikāval for the next year and from the third year onwards 60 kalam of paddy per vēli besides pāđikāval. It is specifically stated that the said endowment was of the kuđinīnkāt-tēvadāņam nature.

cells.king: Kūđalā|āppiiandān Kōpperuñjingadēva (Kōpperuñjinga II)
cells.date: r.y. —: (aec. A.D. 1243)
cells.remarks: Later Pallava; Sakalabhuvaṇachakravartti Kūđalā|āppiiandān Kōpperuñjingadēva (Kōpperuñjinga II), r.y. —: (aec. A.D. 1243). Mentions gifts of different ornaments to the deities in the (Śīva) temple at Tiruvanṇamalai such as ear ornament (kāđṇkambi) crown (kadirmaṇimakuṭam) bāhuvalayam, foot-ornament, vā|i, aureole (tiruvāśi), throne, etc., made of gold, precious stones and pearls by the chief, referred to as Mallai-kāvalaṇ, Nichchaṇka-mallaṇ, Pallavar-vēndaṇ and Baratam-vallāṇ. Also records the charitable activities of his son Vēṇavuđaiyāṇ,1 like bul lding of Avaṇiā|āppirāndāṇ-maṇđapa, Kāṇgēyaṇ-maṭha, Vā|vallaperumā| garden (tōppu), Tami|ṇnāđukāttaperumā| pond (taṭākam), Vā|vallaperumā| well, Nichchaṇgamallaṇēri and gift or ornaments etc. Mentions Vēṇavuđayāṇ, son of Kōpperuñjinga was the lord of Mallai, Mayilai, Kāṇchī, Taṇđaka-nāđu, Kóval etc., and mentions Nārpattenṇāyiravar. Note: 1. The claims to have driven the 'Te|uṅgar' to the north to perish, Veṇkayya thinks, might refer to his fighting against the Kākatiyas who, during the time of Gaṇapati, took possession of Kāñchipuram (IA, xxi, p. 197). Venkayya believed that the victor was one of the princes who took advantage of the subsequent weakness of the Kākatiyas, and was able to go as far as Drākshārāmam itself. In this view Kōpperuñjingas of Kāñchipuram, Drākshārāman and Tripurāntakam were identical (see, Rangacharya, TLIM, i, p. 85).

cells.remarks: Records that Šannaṇ, the son of Akala-rikattuvarāyar, who was a kāvidi (chief) of the Koṇđar of Perunagar-agaram, and a servant of Pirudi-Gaṅgaraiyar,1 died while fighting relentlessly (taļarā) when the army of the Noļambaṇ2 came and lifted the cattle of Āmaiyūr in Mēl-Āđaiyār-nāđu, a s.d. of Pađuvūr-kōtĵtam. Note: 1. It is more reasonable to identify Pirudi-Gaṅgaraiyar with the Paṅgaļa-nāđu cheif than with the Western Gaṅga cheif Prīthvĵpati I, since the modern Vellore and Pōļūr taluks of the North Arcot district were known as Paṅgaļa-nāđu in inscriptions and ruled by line of cheifs known as Prīthvigaṅgaraiyar.2. The Noļamba (king) may be identified with Mahēndra (I) (latest date Š. 817) son of Puļalchoĝa.

Note: 1. It is more reasonable to identify Pirudi-Gaṅgaraiyar with the Paṅgaļa-nāđu cheif than with the Western Gaṅga cheif Prīthvĵpati I, since the modern Vellore and Pōļūr taluks of the North Arcot district were known as Paṅgaļa-nāđu in inscriptions and ruled by line of cheifs known as Prīthvigaṅgaraiyar.2. The Noļamba (king) may be identified with Mahēndra (I) (latest date Š. 817) son of Puļalchoĝa.

cells.remarks: The multilated Sanskrit portion contains a short genealogical account of the Gaṅgēya family; Mādhava; his son was one renowned as the splitter of a stone-pillar; in this family was born a king 'whose name is given in the corrupt term of Ativarmaṇ, which may be meant for Atrivarmaṇ, Aggivarmaṇ, Arivarmaṇ, etc.'; another king (name lost); then Rājāditya. The Tamil portion states that in the eighth year of king Vijaya Kampa, after Prithvigaṅgaraiyar1 had died, the latter's son, Rājāditya2 caused a temple of īśva a and a house for the deceased (i.e., a tomb atita-garam) to be built on the spot where his father had been buied (palļi-peđuttavi-đattu). Note: 1. Prithvigaṅgaraiyar, of this record must be different from the Gaṅga chief Prithvīpati I, because the latter was the father of Māra-siṅha and the son of Śivamāra (See SII, ii, p. 380) while the former was the father of Rājāditya and apparently the son of the king whose name is hidden in the corrupt form of Ativarmaṇ. He may be identified with a member of the Paṅgaļa-nāđu chiefs who bore the surname Prithvigaṅgaraiyar and was a loyal feudatory under the Pallavas.2. It is better to take Rājāditya Mahādēva, as Mahādēva, son of Rājāditya who assumed the title Prithvigaṅgaraiyar built the sepulchral shrine in memory of his father.

The land was bought by the donor from the sabhā of Vēlūr alias Paramēśvara-maṅgalam. The sabhā of Kāñchivāyil and the sabhā of Nīđūr permitted the water from their respective tanks to be used for irrigating the above land. The sabhā of Vēlūr after receiving enough money from the donor towards the land, declared it tax-free.

cells.remarks: Records that, while Attimallar alias Kaṇṇaradēva-Prīthvigaṅgaraiyar was ruling Kaĵleđuppur - majjadi (Kaĵleđuppūrmaryādā), his subordinate officer Puttađikaĵ alias Aĵivina Kaĵakaṇta-Prīthvigaṅgaraiyaṇ made two endowments of 90 sheep each for two perpetual lamps, one each for the god Nandikampīśvaradēvar and the Guṇamalaip Perumaṇ of Kātṭuttūmbūr. These endowments were entrusted to the nagaram of the village. The same officer further made the gift of a kalañju of gold for supplying one ulakku each of the tumbai flowers to the gods. He also donated a village Amalañgavali Attimañgala-chaturvēdimañ alam formed by clubbing four villages into one, with the consent of his master Prithvigañgaraiyar, for providing food offerings to the god Guṇamalaip-Perumāñ during all the three services.

cells.match: <button type="button" class="xref-link" data-corpus="sii" data-key="sii|vii||442" data-url="SII-Inscriptions.html">SII Vol. VII, No. 442</button>
cells.remarks: Begins with the historical introduction Tiṇgaļēr malarndu etc., of the inscription of the king. Registers sale of 1,932 kuļi of land by the mahāsabhā of Ulagaļanda-choļa-chaturvēdimaṅgalam in Šeṅguṇṭra-nāđu in Palkuṇṭak-kōtṭtam a s.d. of Jayaṅgoṇđa-choļa-maṇđalam to the temple of Tirukkārīśvara on receipt of 10 kaļaṇju of gold, from the kaṇmigaļ of the temple, the fineness of which was comparable to that of kuđiñaikkal. The land was declared tax-free, by the mahāsabhā peruṅkuṛi. The deed was written by the madhyastha Kuṭṭēṛaṇ Ānandakkūttaṇ alias Āyiratteṇmat-Tiri-chchiṛambala Alaṅkārappiriyaṇ. Among the boundaries are mentioned Śrī-Arumiṭi dēva-vati, Ulagaṅandachōlā-vāyakkāl etc.

Gives detailed list of the lands with their extent specified in each case, which had been endowed to the temple for its various requirements and recorded on its wall prior to its renovation by Tiru-chchigrambalamuđaiyāñ Tirunagaidēvañ alias Šembiyañ Mūvēndavēļāñ of Ālattūr in Ālattūrnāđu, a s.d. of Nittavinōda-vaļanāđu in Chōļa-manđalam and which were now confirmed by the urār of the place.2

Note: 1. Mistake for Parakēsarivarmañ.2. A few donors of the lands mentioned in the list also figure as signatories at the end of the record.

cells.remarks: The Sanskrit portion opens with an invocation to Vishnu. The next veise celebrates Āditya (I), surnamed Vīranārāyaṇa. He granted the revenue from (a field called) Vaṁśavāri in favour of a tank named Chōlavāridi. This Parāntaka (I), had conferred the title 'lord of the Bāṇas' (Bānādhirāja), on Prithvipati of the Gaṅga race, who was surnamed Hastimalla and defeated an unnamed enemy in the battle of Vallāla.1 At his request, the king entrusted him with the execution of the grant. Next follows the usual capetio benevolentiae in which Hastimalla is called Vīra-Chōla. The last verse states that these verses were composed by the Vaikhānaśa Kumāra of the Kāśyapagōtra. The Tamil portion records that Hastimalla, surnamed Vīra-Chōla, the king of Parivai and vassal of the Chōla king, executed the royal grant by assigning the paddy-field named Mūngilvari (to the tank). Note: 1. For a discussion on the battle of Vallāla see EI, xxvi, p. 114.

cells.remarks: Seems to refer to some provision for two perpetual lamps. One of the fragments mentions [Śi]raimīṭṭaperumā|2 alias Sīya- Another inscription from Mē|pāḍi, dated in the 8th year of Rājārāja III i.e. A.D. 1224), mentions Śiraimiṭṭa-Perumā| alias Sīyagaṅgadēvar as the nephew of Madhurāntaka-ppottappichchōlāṇ Pudōļi-araśaṇ who is stated therein to have erected a maṇdapa for Chōlēndraśiņga-nāyaka. Evidently Šīyagangaṇ alias Šīgaimītjta-perumāļ of the record under review and his name sake of the inscriptions from Kāņchī-puram and Mēlpāđi are identical. The name Chōlēndrasirnha seems to lend some support to the view recorded in the Guruparamparāprabhāva that the modern name of Šōļiņgapuram is derived from Chōlēndraśirnhapuram so named after a king who had Chōlēndrasirnha as his title and was responsible for the prosperity of this ancient place. Šīyagaņga's father apparently adopted the title Chōlēndrasirnha in imitation of a Chōlā king, whose identity is not known. Note: 1. The record is written in characters of the 13th cent. A.D.2. In a record from Kāñchipuram (ARE, 1919, no. 289) dated in the 35th regnal year of Tribhuvaṇavīradēva (Kulōttunga III), i.e., A.D. 1213 one Sīyagaṅga is mentioned as having constructed the shrine of Anantā|vār in stone. He also bears, among others, the title Śiraimiṭṭa-perumā| and his father is called Chō|endrasirnha.

In a record from Kāñchipuram (ARE, 1919, no. 289) dated in the 35th regnal year of Tribhuvaṇavīradēva (Kulōttunga III), i.e., A.D. 1213 one Sīyagaṅga is mentioned as having constructed the shrine of Anantā|vār in stone. He also bears, among others, the title Śiraimiṭṭa-perumā| and his father is called Chō|endrasirnha.

cells.remarks: Records that under the orders of the mahā-sabhā of Kāvadippākkam alias Amaṇinārāyaṇa-chatuvēdimaṅgalam, in Paṭuvurkōṭtam, constituted of the greatmen of kuḍumbu-vārikam, tōṭṭavārikam, kaṭaṇi-vārikam, and vaṭakaṭaṇi-varikam and the bhṭṭas and viśisṭās, the members of ērivārikam received 120 kaṭaṇju of gold of 9½ mārī of fineness from Tīraṇ-Chēṇnippēra-raiyar of Araiśūr in Pāmbuṇi-kūṭgam, a s.d. of Chōṭa-nāḍu, as capital for paying the ferry-men (ōḍa-nāyaṇmār) engaged in raising the bund of the big tank of the village. A portion of the interest on the gold was set apart for feeding for apūrvi brāhmaṇas well versed in the Vēdas in the feeding-hall (śālai-maṇḍagam) built by the donor in the temple of Tirukkarapuram situated on the bank of the Pāryāṇu in the village. The latter charity was instituted by the donor in commemoration of four of his soldiers (śevagar) who died when the donor (probably a commander of the army) made a frontal attack (neṛrīśēṇrā) on the occasion when the Pāṇdya king and the king of ṭijam1 marched against Perumānaḍigaṛ (i.e. Parāntaka I) and fought with him a deadly battle (asti-gaḍai-chevda-ñāṇṭu)2 at Vēṭur.3 Note: 1. The Ceylonese king did not come to the fight himself according to the Mahāvarīsa.2. It may also mean 'a fight on elephants'; see also ARE, 1926, no. 231. The Pāṇdya did not die as stated in ARE, 1926, part ii, para 16.3. The date of about A.D. 915, has been suggested for this battle (Cf. Cōṭas, 1955 edn. p. 123)

cells.remarks: Chōļa; Parakēsarivarmaṇ, r.y. 5: (10th cent. A.D.). Records an agreement by the mahāsabhā of Kāvidippākkam alias Amaninārāyaṇa-chaturvēdimaṅgalam in Pađuvūr-koṭṭam through their tank supervision committee to burn a perpetual lamp in the local temple of Tirukkarapurattu-Perumāna-digaļ and in that of Tiruvagattiśvarattu-Perumāna-digaļ at Pākkam. For the former they received a piece of garden-land endowed by one Śivapūdi Āchchanāđaṇ, son of Mahāśēna-kramavittar and for the latter, a gift of 50 (kāśu) of pure gold from Šembiyaṇ Iļaṅgōvēļār Pūdi Ādittar. Mention is made of certain aṅgamaṇi-dravya (cash realised by sale of ornaments) which was the property of the donor s (deceased mother) out of which he is said to have purchased the land endowed. An executive official servant of the sabhā called the Śirṭūātchikoļvāṇ who was appointed for the year, was to look after the maintenance of the gift. Note: 1. This donor is evidently a Kođumbāļūr chief-tain cf no. NA-997 above.

cells.remarks: Records a sale of 700 kuļi of dry land by public auction to PaṇaikiJāṇ Vađugaṇ Vāṇādarājāṇ of Koṭṭaiyūr in Vādavūrnāđu a s.d. of Veṇkuṇṇak-kōṭṭam for five gaṇđagōpāluṇ-māđai (vāś pađā pudumāđai) by the seven sons of Mūprāla Amritārya Sarvamahākrituyājiyār of Pullapākkam alias Dhanmasūrach-chaturvēdimaṅgaļam in Kāśirampeđu-nāđu, a s.d. of Kāliyūr-kōṭṭam in Jayañkoṇđachōļa-maṇđalam. The said land was obtained by them as a gift (daṇmādaṇam) from the residents (ūravar) of Sakkaramūdūr, an independent village (taṇiyūr) of Dāmar-kōṭṭam. The seven sons mentioned are: (i) Nārāyaṇabhaṭṭaṇ; (ii) Yajñamūrttibhaṭṭaṇ; (iii) Nārāyaṇabhaṭṭaṇ; (iv) Šingapirāṇbhaṭṭaṇ; (v) Periyapperumāļ; (vi) Tiruvaraṅgaṇ; and (vii) Gövindaṇ. On behalf of (v) and (vi) (being minor sons ?) their uncle, Aruļājabhaṭṭa of Gōmapuram, signed the document as their guardian (mudukaṇ). Note: 1. The date falls in the 17th regnal year of the king and the regnal year quoted in the epigraph is an expired one.

Registers gift of the tank called Araiyaṇ-ēri and the paddy cultivation land irrigated by the tank, free of taxes, to the temple of Tiruvanantiśvaram-Uđaiyār at Vādavūr in Vādavūr-nāđu, a s.d. of Veṇkuṇṇak-kōṭṭam by the ūrār of the village. States that those who opposed the order were liable to the punishment meted out to persons who disobeyed the royal order.

Note: 1. Read as Rājakēsarivarmaṇ in the above Epigraphy Report.

cells.reference: ARE, 1919, no. 254; Ibid, part ii, para 21.
cells.remarks: Registers a compact entered into between Kṇḍal-Araṣanārāyaṇaṇ Ālappirandāṇ alias Kulōttuṅgachōĵa-Śambuvarāyar by which both swore that they shou'd not do anything that would be detrimental to the interests of either; that the latter should not form any alliance with Ālappirandāṇ Edirilichōĵa-Śambuvarāyaṇ; that he should confine himself to certain specified tracts of country which if he transgressed, the mudalis would send up arms and horses and cause him injury; that if Ālappirandāṇ Edirilichōĵa-Śambuvarāyaṇ inflicted any trouble on Kulōttuṅgachōĵa-Śambuvarāyaṇ, Kāḍavarāyaṇ would support him; that in case Ālappirandāṇ Edirilichōĵa-Śambuvarāyaṇ ran away from his hill (residence) leaving behind him all arms, Kulōttuṅgachōĵa-Śambuvarāyaṇ should have possession of them subject to the condition that he would not shelter or form any alliance with the other and that if Kāḍavarayaṇ allied himself with the relatives of Kulōttuṅgachōĵa-Śambuvarāyaṇ and with Ālappirandāṇ Edirilichōĵa-Śambuvarāyaṇ against the interests of Kulōttuṅgachōĵa-Śambuvarāyaṇ, he (Kāḍavarāyaṇ) would demean himself to the position of carrying the sandals of his enemies and of eating the chewed betel leaves thrown out from their mouths.

cells.remarks: Pāņdya; Perumā! Kulašēkharadēva, (Mārāvarmaņ Kulašēkhara I?),1 r.y. 16= (c A.D. 1284). States that Vijayapālaņ of Puduppākkam made an ornamental pedestal and had the god installed on it. Note: 1. There were three Pāņdya kings by name Kulašākhara coming into picture in the 13th cent. A.D. The earliest of them viz. Jaṭāvarmaņ Kulašēkhara I (acc. A.D. 1190) confined himself to the Pāņdya country and the second one Jaṭāvarmaņ Kulašākhara II, (acc. c A.D. 1238) is known to have ruled only for seven years. Hence this record may be attributed to Mārāvarmaņ Kulašēkhara I (acc. c A.D. 1268).

It is stated that the gold shall not become the commodity (?) of goldsmiths.

cells.remarks: Records the endowment by the ūrār of Śāttamaṅgalam for the tank (in the village). The endowment consisted of two paṭṭi of aṭrappuṭam and in Īttaṅkāḍu, two paṭṭi of iļamakkaļ-paṭṭi, (the income from the taxes of) kūṭtu, irappu, iļamakkaļ-kāṇam, [mattu]-nel (?) and pānilai (?), three house sites and the palmyra grove in the eastern field included under Mudukāḍu. The iļamakkaļ and not the maṇṭrāḍuvār are stated to be the nāyakar (administrators ?) (of the endowment). The ūrār agreed that sellers and purchasers of the endowed property, if any, shall pay a fine of 100 kaļānju to the temple.

cells.remarks: Records gift of a cheṛuvu of land and a well to the temple of Tirukkarĵraļi-Mahādēva at Šīyamangalam as dēvadāna to provide for oļukkavi offerings. The donor seems to be Šrī-Gaṅgaraiyar Gaṅga-Chūlāmani alias Mummuđichōla-Šembiyaṇ Šrī Gaṅgaraiyar of Neđunguṅrgam in Kuṅrga-nāđu, a s.d. Palakuṅrgak-kōtĵtam, who was ruling over Palakuṅrga-kōtĵtam, Veṅkuṅrgak-kōtĵtam and Šingapura-nāđu. The ūr of the village remitted all kinds of taxe, on the granted land including irai, echchōrgu, vetĵti and amañji. It is stated that on default, the ūr as a whole were liable to a daily fine of 108 kāṇam at the dharmāsana and daily fine of 24¼ (kāṇam) from the kuđikkāđu; and for obstruction of irrigation channels or water, they were liable to another fine of ¼ pon daily to the ruler of the day.

text.remarks: Records gift of a cheṛuvu of land and a well to the temple of Tirukkarĵraļi-Mahādēva at Šīyamangalam as dēvadāna to provide for oļukkavi offerings. The donor seems to be Šrī-Gaṅgaraiyar Gaṅga-Chūlāmani alias Mummuđichōla-Šembiyaṇ Šrī Gaṅgaraiyar of Neđunguṅrgam in Kuṅrga-nāđu, a s.d. Palakuṅrgak-kōtĵtam, who was ruling over Palakuṅrga-kōtĵtam, Veṅkuṅrgak-kōtĵtam and Šingapura-nāđu. The ūr of the village remitted all kinds of taxe, on the granted land including irai, echchōrgu, vetĵti and amañji. It is stated that on default, the ūr as a whole were liable to a daily fine of 108 kāṇam at the dharmāsana and daily fine of 24¼ (kāṇam) from the kuđikkāđu; and for obstruction of irrigation channels or water, they were liable to another fine of ¼ pon daily to the ruler of the day.

cells.remarks: Records gift of 1,602 kuļi of land by Kađamban Vēnkađan a veļļāla of Nallūr-udukkuđi in Tiruvijundūrnāđu situated on the southern (bank) of Chōļa-nāđu, for two perpetual lamps. The land was previously sold to the donor by the ūr of Šīyamangalam in Teṇṇār-nāđu, in Palkuṇra-kōtṭam and was freed from all taxes and dues. The gifted land was taken charge by the ūr for cultivation who agreed therefor, to supply daily one uri of oil, for two lamps, the quantity of which was comparable to that of the measure nāļi of the god who was pleased to stand at Kachchippēđu (ūragattu-niṇrār-nāļi) to god Tirukkar-ja-Mahādēvar of the village. Mentions 16 span rod, 4 span rod, and Ambalattādī-vāyakkāl and Veṇkāđadēva-vāykkāl.

cells.match_text: ARE 1921-22, App. B, No. 418; SII Vol. XII Pt I, No. 128
cells.remarks: The beginning prose passage refers to Kōpperuñjingañ Aļagiyasīyañ who conquered the Chōļa king at Teļļāru, deprived him of all royal insignia, and after imprisoning the Chōļā king, took the Chōļa country. The first verse extols the greatness and prowess of Kōpperuñjingadēva in accomplishing the imprisonment of the Chōļa king along with his ministers and annexing the Chōļa territory, and further, it refers to his encounter with Hoysāļa warriors, his vast army, his favourite deity in the Golden Hall at Chidambaram and to his love for and patronage of Tamil literature. The second verse warns other kings not to oppose this chief but to submit themselves quietly by paying tribute, considering the fate of the Chōļa king. The next verse, after referring to the exploits of this ruler in stamping the insignia of his banner on the breast and shoulders of powerful kings refers to the langour of the Chōļa sovereign in prison. The last two verses are addressed directly to the king describing the state of his lady-love during his absence on a campaign against the Chōļa king.

The Sanskrit portion of the grant gives the mythical genealogy of the Pallavas from Note: 1. These plates have been noticed by Sewell as available in the Collector's office of North Arcot district. cells.location: B. A COPPER PLATE INSCRIPTION OF RĀJA VĪRA CHĒŁA · Wandiwash Taluk · North Arcot · Tamil Nadu
cells.findspot: Received from the collector's office, North Arcot district and now deposited in the Govt. Museum, Egmore, Madras
cells.dynasty: ChĒła
cells.king: Rāja Vīra ChĒła
cells.date: Ś 1008 or 1011=A.D. 1066 or 1089
cells.reference: Rober Sewell, List of Antiquities, Madras, ii, p. 1-2; TLIMP, i, p. 31.
cells.remarks: ChĒła; Rāja Vīra ChĒła; r.y.—, Ś 1008 or 1011=A.D. 1066 or 1089.1 This is one of a very curious series of 13 plates, all from the same locality. They all purport to be grants by a ChĒła sovereign in the years Ś. 1008 or 1011, to which period they cannot palaeographically belong. Moreover, they bear a seal at the top in characters resembling the Persian and this would seem to be a clear anachronism. This grant is on a leaden plate, coated with a thin sheet of copper. It purports to be a grant by Rāja Vīra ChĒła in Ś. 1011 in the year of Kaliyuga 4190 and cyclic year Plavaṅga. "It seems difficult to suppose that all these plates can be forgeries, partly from their number, and partly because no forger would be so foolish as to annex the Persian seal to such a document. The only other explanation that seems reasonable is that they form a series of copies of older authentic documents, recording grants confirmed by the Muhammadan chief at the time the copies were taken, and therefore bearing his seal." Note: 1. The year 1089 A.D. corresponds with the twenty-fifth year of the reign of the sovereign variously known as "Vīra ChĒła", "Rāja Vīra", "Rāja Rājēndra", "Kulōttunga" and "Koppara Kesarivarman" (Kō-Parakēsarivarman).2. This year S.S. 1011 corresponds to the cyclic year Sukla, twenty-two years subsequent to Plavaṅga.
